notes.title: The largest empty circle is not always centred at an intersection
notes.text: The video says the centre will always be at an intersection. Without a bounded region, the maximum can be unbounded. In a bounded region, a boundary point can be optimal. The local syllabus guidance specifies examination questions where the solution is at an intersection of three edges.

ican.text: I can identify sites, cells, edges and vertices and interpret a cell in context.
I can find and restrict a boundary using perpendicular bisectors and nearest-site comparisons.
I can update a diagram when a site is added and calculate a cell area in a stated bounded region.
I can use nearest-neighbour interpolation and explain its assumptions and limitations.
I can compare candidate locations for a largest-empty-circle problem, including domain boundaries when required.

ku.text: A site is a fixed location. Its Voronoi cell consists of all points at least as close to that site as to every other site. In the interior, it is the unique nearest site; on a shared edge, two or more sites tie for nearest.

In the usual planar Euclidean model, an edge separating two distinct sites lies on their perpendicular bisector. The whole bisector is not automatically an edge: retain only points no farther from those two sites than from any other site.

A Voronoi vertex is a point where edges meet. At an ordinary three-site vertex, the point is equally distant from those three nearest sites. Other sites must be no closer. Special configurations can have four or more sites tied.

To locate a point, compare distances or squared distances to all sites. Squared distances preserve order because distances are nonnegative. A tie means the point is on a shared boundary, not strictly inside one cell.

To add a site, compare its distance with each old site. Its new cell is the intersection of the corresponding nearer-or-equal half-planes, clipped to the domain if one is given. Existing cells lose points where the new site is closer; keep only valid edge portions.

For a bounded diagram, find a cell’s vertices in order, including intersections with the domain boundary, then use geometric decomposition or a coordinate-area method. State square units and avoid including regions assigned to another site.

Nearest-neighbour interpolation assigns a location the recorded value of its nearest site. On a tie, specify a tie-breaking rule or report the ambiguity. The estimate assumes the nearest measurement is informative; spatial proximity alone does not establish accuracy.

The largest-empty-circle or maximin location maximises the distance to the nearest site over an allowed set of centres. In a bounded region, possible maxima include relevant Voronoi vertices, intersections with the region boundary and domain corners. Compare their nearest-site distances.

In the local AI syllabus guidance, examination questions specify a solution at an intersection of three edges. That is a question-specific restriction, not a general theorem. With no bounded domain, a finite largest empty circle need not exist.
The meaning of distance matters. A diagram based on straight-line Euclidean distance need not identify the quickest route when roads, obstacles or travel times matter.

misc.weak: Every point on the bisector of two sites is a Voronoi edge.
misc.better: A third site may be closer. Keep only points where the tied pair are nearest.

misc.weak: The nearest site to a point on an edge is unique.
misc.better: The adjoining sites tie there; at a vertex three or more can tie.

misc.weak: The largest empty circle must always have its centre at a Voronoi vertex.
misc.better: Check the allowed region. A boundary or corner can be optimal, and an unrestricted plane need not have a finite optimum.

misc.weak: Nearest-neighbour interpolation averages all site values.
misc.better: Use the value at the nearest site, with an explicit rule for ties.

misc.weak: When a new site is added, draw its entire pairwise bisectors as edges.
misc.better: Restrict each bisector to points where the new site and its neighbour are jointly closest to all sites.

terms.text: A fixed location used to define a nearest-site region.
The set of locations nearest to a given site, including ties on its boundary under the closed-cell convention.
A boundary portion where neighbouring sites tie for nearest.
A point where Voronoi edges meet, usually equidistant from three nearest sites.
Estimating a value using the recorded value at the nearest site.
A circle whose interior contains no site, chosen with the largest radius among permitted centres.

formula.text: Compare sites $A$ and $B$ at $(x,y)$ by comparing their squared distances: $(x-x_A)^2+(y-y_A)^2$ and $(x-x_B)^2+(y-y_B)^2$.
Their pairwise bisector satisfies $d_A^2=d_B^2$. Retain only the portion where no other site is closer.
For a chosen centre $P$, the radius of the largest circle centred at $P$ with no site in its interior is $\min_i d(P,S_i)$.

worked.prompt: A square study area is $0\leq x\leq8$, $0\leq y\leq8$, with distances in kilometres. Three monitoring sites are $A=(2,2)$, $B=(6,2)$ and $C=(4,6)$. Their rainfall readings are $60$, $75$ and $90$ mm, respectively. Use straight-line distance.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the pairwise bisectors and their common intersection.
parts.a: The midpoint of $AB$ is $(4,2)$ and $AB$ is horizontal, so its bisector is $x=4$. Equating squared distances gives the other two bisectors $y=5.5-\frac{x}{2}$ for $A,C$ and $y=1.5+\frac{x}{2}$ for $B,C$. They meet at $V=(4,3.5)$. At $V$ all three squared distances are $6.25$, so this is a three-site Voronoi vertex.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Describe the boundaries of the cell for $C$ within the square and find its area.
parts.a: $C$ is at least as close as $A$ when $y\geq5.5-x/2$ and at least as close as $B$ when $y\geq1.5+x/2$. Thus its lower boundary runs from $(0,5.5)$ to $(4,3.5)$ to $(8,5.5)$; the top is $y=8$. Divide the cell into two trapezia with parallel vertical sides $2.5$ and $4.5$ km and width $4$ km. Each has area $\frac12(2.5+4.5)(4)=14\text{ km}^2$, so the total is $28\text{ km}^2$.

parts.label: c
parts.q: Estimate rainfall at $P=(4,5)$ using nearest-neighbour interpolation.
parts.a: $PC=1$ km while $PA=PB=\sqrt{13}$ km. The nearest site is $C$, so the nearest-neighbour estimate is $90$ mm. It is an estimate based on the chosen method, not a measured value at $P$.

parts.label: d
parts.q: A new site $D=(4,2)$ is added. Describe the three new edges of its cell inside the square.
parts.a: The $A,D$ bisector is $x=3$ and the $B,D$ bisector is $x=5$. The $C,D$ bisector is $y=4$. Comparing all four sites restricts the new cell to $3\leq x\leq5$ and $0\leq y\leq4$. Its new inter-site edges are $x=3$ for $0\leq y\leq4$, $x=5$ for $0\leq y\leq4$ and $y=4$ for $3\leq x\leq5$. The side on $y=0$ is the study-area boundary.

parts.label: e
parts.q: Find the new area of the cell for $C$ after adding $D$.
parts.a: The new constraint for $C$ is $y\geq4$. It removes from the old cell the triangle with vertices $(3,4)$, $(4,3.5)$ and $(5,4)$, of area $\frac12(2)(0.5)=0.5\text{ km}^2$. The new area is $28-0.5=27.5\text{ km}^2$.

parts.label: f
parts.q: Before adding $D$, compare $V$ with the corner $K=(0,8)$ as centres for an empty circle. Does this example show why domain boundaries matter?
parts.a: At $V$, the nearest-site distance is $2.5$ km. At $K$, the squared distances to $A,B,C$ are $40,72,20$, so the nearest site is $C$ and the radius is $\sqrt{20}$ km. Since $\sqrt{20}>2.5$, $V$ is not the best of these two candidates. A boundary candidate can be better than an interior Voronoi vertex; this comparison alone does not prove the global optimum.

kq.q: Why must a bisector be tested against the other sites?
kq.model: It shows a tie between two sites, but another site may be nearer. A Voronoi edge requires the tied sites to be nearest as well.

kq.q: Why does adding a site change existing cells?
kq.model: Locations closer to the new site than their former nearest site move into the new cell. The remaining portions keep their nearest old site.

kq.q: Why do domain boundaries matter for the largest empty circle?
kq.model: A centre restricted to a bounded region can be farthest from all sites on the region boundary or at a corner. The candidates depend on the allowed region.
It uses the nearest site’s value as a local estimate. It assumes proximity is a useful guide; an edge tie or sharp local variation may make the estimate less reliable.
